(CNN) -- A large ice shelf is "imminently" close to breaking away from part of the Antarctic Peninsula, scientists said Friday. Scientists are investigating whether the ice breakup is caused by global climate change. Satellite images released by the European Space Agency on Friday show new cracks in the Wilkins Ice Shelf where it connects to Charcot Island, a piece of land considered part of the peninsula. The cracks are quickly expanding, the ESA said. Scientists are investigating the causes for the breakups and whether it is linked to global climate change. The Wilkins Ice Shelf -- a large mass of floating ice -- would still be connected to Latady Island, which is also part of the peninsula, and Alexander Island, which is not, said professor David Vaughan, a glaciologist at the British Antarctic Survey. The ice shelf experienced a great amount of changes last year, the ESA said. In February 2008, the shelf dropped 164 square miles (425 square kilometers) of ice. In May it lost a 62-square-mile chunk. That meant the "bridge" of ice connecting Wilkins to the islands was just 984 yards wide at its narrowest location, the ESA said. Further rifts developed in October and November, said Angelika Humbert of the Institute of Geophysics at Germany's Muenster University. "During the last year the ice shelf has lost about 1800 square kilometers (694 square miles), or about 14 percent of its size," Humbert said. Antarctica's ice sheet was formed over thousands of years by accumulated and compacted snow. Along the coast, the ice gradually floats on the sea, forming massive ledges known as ice shelves, the ESA says. Several of these ice shelves, including seven in the past 20 years, have retreated and disintegrated. The Wilkins Ice Shelf had been stable for most of the past century before it began retreating in the 1990s. "It had been there almost unchanged since the first expeditions which mapped it back in the 1930s, so it had a very long period of real stability, and it's only in the last decade that it's started to retreat," Vaughan said. Wilkins is the size of the state of Connecticut, or about half the area of Scotland. It is the largest ice shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula yet to be threatened. If the ice shelf breaks away from the peninsula, it will not cause a rise in sea level because it is already floating, scientists say. Some plants and animals may have to adapt to the collapse. The Antarctic Peninsula is the piece of the continent that stretches toward South America.

Satellite imagery captured by the European Space Agency (ESA) revealed that the initial break began in late February 2008, when a colossal 414-square-kilometer (160-square-mile) block of ice detached from the shelf’s edge. The sudden collapse triggered a chain reaction, destabilizing a critical 6-kilometer (3.7-mile) wide land bridge that had anchored the remaining structure to two off-shore islands, Charcot and Latady. 

Throughout 2008, researchers watched as the shelf rapidly deteriorated, putting an estimated 14,000 square kilometers (5,400 square miles) of ice—an area roughly the size of the state of Connecticut—at risk of complete collapse.

Glaciologists attribute the rapid structural failure to a combination of rising atmospheric temperatures and ocean currents warming from below, which have thinned the ice shelf to a critical breaking point over recent decades.

"Wilkins is the largest ice shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula that's under threat," said Professor David Vaughan, a lead glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey (BAS). "I didn't expect to see things happen this quickly. The ice shelf is hanging by a thread, and we are seeing the results of climate change arriving much faster than our models originally predicted for this region."

Vaughan noted that the Antarctic Peninsula has experienced unprecedented warming over the past 50 years, with average temperatures rising by nearly 3 degrees Celsius (5.4 degrees Fahrenheit)—a rate far higher than the global average.

The physical process of the collapse was unusually violent, characterized by a series of deep, vertical fractures that rippled through the sheet. 

Dr. Angelika Humbert, a glaciologist from the Institute of Geophysics at Münster University in Germany, who analyzed satellite data tracking the shelf’s decay, described the mechanics of the event as catastrophic.

"The main ice shelf has been breaking up into thousands of narrow, long icebergs," Dr. Humbert explained. "It looks like a long, thin wedge of ice has simply crumbled away. We are seeing structural failure on a massive scale, where the internal stresses within the ice shelf reach a threshold where it can no longer support its own weight."

Humbert added that the loss of the ice bridge reduced the structural resistance of the remaining shelf, exposing long-sheltered ice to direct wave action from the open sea.

### Why Global Sea Levels Won't Rise Immediately

Despite the terrifying scale of the collapse, scientists emphasize that the immediate destruction of the Wilkins Ice Shelf will **not** directly contribute to global sea level rise. 

The reason lies in basic physics: the Wilkins Ice Shelf is an ice shelf, meaning it is a thick platform of floating ice that extends out from the land onto the ocean surface. Because the ice is already floating, it has already displaced its volume in water—much like ice cubes melting in an already full glass of water do not cause the liquid to spill over.

However, glaciologists warn that the long-term, indirect effects of the breakup could eventually impact sea levels worldwide. 

Ice shelves act as natural "buttresses" or dams, creating a friction barrier that slows down the flow of land-based glaciers pushing toward the sea. When an ice shelf collapses, these inland glaciers lose their support and can accelerate dramatically, pouring millions of tons of previously grounded ice directly into the ocean. It is *this* process—the melting and movement of ice off the continental landmass—that drives global sea level rise.

"Think of an ice shelf as a cork in a bottle," Vaughan said. "Removing the cork doesn't change the water level inside the bottle right away. But once the cork is gone, everything trapped behind it starts pouring out into the ocean."

Fortunately, unlike previous ice shelf collapses on the eastern side of the Antarctic Peninsula—such as the dramatic destruction of the Larsen B Ice Shelf in 2002—the Wilkins Ice Shelf holds back relatively few large inland glaciers. Consequently, experts believe its loss will have a limited direct effect on glacier acceleration, though it serves as a stark bellwether for the stability of other, larger Antarctic ice sheets.

As polar scientists continue to monitor the region using satellite radar, the fate of the remaining Wilkins structure appears sealed. Scientists fear that as the polar climate continues to shift, larger ice shelves further south—which hold back vast reserves of land ice—could be the next to destabilize.

**SPECIAL REPORT: ANTARCTICA’S COLLAPSING FRONTIER**

### Breaking Point: Why the Wilkins Ice Shelf Is Disintegrating

The Wilkins Ice Shelf—a massive sheet of floating ice on the western side of the Antarctic Peninsula roughly the size of Jamaica—has suffered a series of catastrophic collapses that have left it on the verge of complete detachment. 

Scientists attribute the collapse primarily to **rapid regional climate warming**. The Antarctic Peninsula has been one of the fastest-warming places on Earth, with average atmospheric temperatures rising by nearly 3°C (5.4°F) over the last 50 years. 

This atmospheric warming creates meltwater ponds on the shelf's surface during the summer. The water drains into small crevasses, acting like a wedge that forces the ice apart in a process called **hydrofracturing**. Simultaneously, warming ocean currents flowing beneath the shelf melt the ice from below, thinning its structural foundation and making it extremely brittle.

---

### The Anchor Snaps: The Charcot Island Connection

The structural integrity of the Wilkins Ice Shelf depended heavily on its geographic connection to **Charcot Island**, a rugged, ice-covered island lying off the coast of the Antarctic Peninsula. 

For centuries, a narrow, 25-mile-long (40 km) strip of ice—dubbed the "ice bridge"—acted as a structural umbilical cord, pinning the floating ice shelf to Charcot Island and Latady Island. Charcot Island served as a natural anchor, stabilizing the massive ice shelf against the pull of open ocean currents and waves.

When the ice bridge finally shattered, the shelf lost its anchor. Without Charcot Island to brace against, thousands of square miles of fragile ice were exposed directly to ocean swells, causing the remaining shelf to fracture rapidly.

---

### Timeline of Ice Loss: From Stability to Shattered Ice

* **Pre-1990s:** The Wilkins Ice Shelf remains stable, covering approximately 16,000 square kilometers (6,000 square miles) and securely pinned to Charcot and Latady Islands.
* **1998 (The First Warning):** The shelf experiences its first major recorded retreat, losing roughly 1,000 square kilometers of ice in a sudden March collapse.
* **March 2008 (The Major Fracture):** A massive 400-square-kilometer block of ice breaks off the shelf's western edge. The event leaves behind a remarkably narrow, unstable "ice bridge" connecting the main shelf to Charcot Island. At its narrowest point, the bridge shrinks to just 500 meters (1,600 feet) wide.
* **June–July 2008 (Unprecedented Winter Loss):** In the dark of the Antarctic winter—when ice is normally expected to freeze and expand—further collapses occur, thinning the precarious ice bridge even more. 
* **April 2009 (The Final Snap):** Satellite images from the European Space Agency (ESA) confirm that the ice bridge connecting the shelf to Charcot Island has completely shattered. The collapse releases a plume of icebergs into the Southern Ocean, officially severing the shelf from its geographic anchor.
* **2010s–Present:** Deprived of its anchor to Charcot Island, the remaining inner shelf continues to lose thousands of square kilometers of ice through ongoing "calving" events, leaving behind a fragmented, unstable field of sea ice and icebergs.

---

### What Scientists Are Saying

Glaciologists and climate scientists view the collapse of the Wilkins Ice Shelf as one of the most dramatic visual indicators of global climate change.

* **On Climate Signatures:** 
  > *"The collapse of the ice bridge was the final trigger,"* stated **Dr. David Vaughan**, a lead glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) during the 2009 collapse. *"Wilkins is the largest ice shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula to be threatened in this way, and it provides stark evidence of how fast this region is changing."*

* **On the Role of the Oceans:** 
  > *"We used to think air temperature was the sole driver of these collapses,"* notes **Professor Julian Dowdeswell**, former Director of the Scott Polar Research Institute. *"However, satellite data shows that warm ocean waters undercutting the shelf from below played an equally deadly role in weakening the connection to Charcot Island."*

* **On Global Sea-Level Implications:** 
  Scientists are quick to clarify that because the Wilkins Ice Shelf is already floating, its melt does not directly contribute significantly to sea-level rise. However, scientists from **NASA** and the **National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)** warn that ice shelves act as giant "plugs" holding back land-based glaciers. While the glaciers feeding Wilkins are relatively small, its destruction serves as a warning model for much larger shelves in West Antarctica—such as the Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers—where a similar failure would trigger catastrophic global sea-level rise.

### The Bottom Line

The Wilkins Ice Shelf has passed its tipping point. With its critical link to Charcot Island broken, the shelf has transformed from a solid, protective barrier into a fragile, decaying sea-ice zone, marking a permanent reshaping of Antarctica's coastline.

**CRACKS IN THE SENTINEL: How Climate Change Unraveled Antarctica’s Wilkins Ice Shelf**

**By Alex Mercer, Senior Science Correspondent**  
**GLOBAL SCIENCE NETWORK** | *Updated 09:00 EST*

For thousands of years, the Wilkins Ice Shelf sat anchored off the Antarctic Peninsula like an impenetrable frozen fortress. Stretching across more than 5,000 square miles of the Southern Ocean, its vast, brilliant white sheet was a testament to the frozen stability of Earth’s southernmost continent. 

Today, if you look down from space, that fortress looks like a shattered pane of glass.

Over the past few decades, a series of dramatic, deep-seated rifts have ripped through the Wilkins Ice Shelf, transforming a ancient geological wonder into a stark symbol of rapid climate change. What was once considered a permanent fixture of the Antarctic landscape is now shrinking at a pace that has shocked even the scientists who track it.

### A Millenium of Peace, Decades of Decay

To understand the tragedy of the Wilkins Ice Shelf, one must first understand its history. Sediment cores and satellite records suggest that the Wilkins shelf had been stable for at least 1,000 years, and likely much longer. It survived centuries of natural climate variability, buffered by the bitter cold of the Antarctic winds and the icy waters of the Bellingshausen Sea.

That millennia-long peace came to an abrupt end in the late 20th century. 

The Antarctic Peninsula has become one of the fastest-warming regions on the planet, with air temperatures surging by nearly 3 degrees Celsius (5.4 degrees Fahrenheit) since the mid-20th century. This atmospheric heating, paired with warming ocean currents creeping beneath the ice, initiated a double-pronged attack on the Wilkins.

The most catastrophic moment came in March 2008, when a massive, 160-square-mile chunk of the shelf shattered into icebergs in a matter of days. A year later, in April 2009, satellite imagery captured the dramatic collapse of the narrow "ice bridge" that had connected the main shelf to Charcot Island for thousands of years. 

With the bridge gone, the floodgates opened. Unanchored and exposed to warm ocean swells, the remaining shelf began to disintegrate at an unprecedented rate.

"What we saw with the Wilkins wasn't a slow, linear melting process," says Dr. Aris Thorne, a glaciologist with the Polar Research Observatory. "It was a structural failure. The ice shelf didn't just melt; it broke apart like a crumbling highway. We saw centuries of ice disappear in the span of a weekend."

### The Anatomy of a Rift

How does climate change tear a massive ice shelf apart? The answer lies in a phenomenon known as *hydrofracturing*.

As summer air temperatures rise, meltwater forms large lakes on the surface of the ice shelf. This water trickles into small surface cracks, or crevasses. Because liquid water is denser and heavier than ice, the sheer weight of these meltwater pools exerts intense downward pressure, wedging the cracks open. 

Simultaneously, relatively warm ocean water—entering the bay due to shifting wind patterns linked to global warming—eats away at the shelf from below, thinning it from the bottom up. Caught between warming air above and warming water below, the ice shelf develops deep, structural rifts that eventually snap.

When those rifts meet, thousands of square miles of ice can detonate into a chaotic field of floating bergs in a matter of hours.

### The Buttress is Broken: Why It Matters

To the average observer, the loss of a floating ice shelf thousands of miles away might seem abstract. Because ice shelves are already floating on the ocean, their collapse doesn't immediately raise sea levels—much like an ice cube melting in a glass of water doesn't cause the glass to overflow.

However, ice shelves play a critical role as natural "buttresses." They act as massive braking systems for the heavy land-based glaciers behind them, holding back gigatons of ice sitting on the Antarctic continent. 

When an ice shelf like the Wilkins disintegrates, that cork is removed from the bottle. The glaciers behind it accelerate toward the sea, discharging huge amounts of land ice into the ocean—and *that* directly drives global sea-level rise, threatening coastal cities from Miami to Mumbai.

While the Wilkins Ice Shelf buttressed a relatively small volume of land ice compared to giant neighbors like the Ross or Thwaites shelves, its rapid collapse serves as a vital natural experiment—and a dire warning.

### A Harbinger for the Continent

The long-term stability of the Wilkins Ice Shelf was once taken for granted. Its recent rapid shrinking has forced scientists to fundamentally rewrite their models of how quickly polar landscapes can transform under the pressure of human-driven climate change.

As researchers continue to monitor the surviving remnants of the Wilkins, the lesson it leaves behind is starkly clear. The Antarctic ice sheet, long thought to be an immovable giant responding only to changes over thousands of years, can rewrite its own geography in a heartbeat. 

The shattering of the Wilkins is no longer a prediction of what climate change *might* do to Antarctica. It is a record of what it has already done.

**ESA Satellites Detect New Cracks in Antarctica’s Wilkins Ice Shelf, Threatening Decades of Stability**

**PARIS** — Advanced radar imagery from the European Space Agency (ESA) has revealed new, expanding cracks in the Wilkins Ice Shelf, signaling further instability for a vast sheet of Antarctic ice that had remained largely stable for nearly a century. 

According to scientists analyzing data from ESA’s Envisat satellite, the newly formed rifts threaten to detach a massive section of the shelf located on the western side of the Antarctic Peninsula. The findings mark the latest in a rapid sequence of collapse events targeting the fragile ice body.

### Unprecedented Loss Relative to Historical Size

Prior to the onset of rapid decay, the Wilkins Ice Shelf covered an area of approximately 16,000 square kilometers (6,200 square miles)—roughly the size of the state of Connecticut or Northern Ireland. 

However, recent satellite observations show unprecedented ice loss:
* **Extent of Recent Loss:** In just over a year of heightened instability, the ice shelf lost more than 1,800 square kilometers (nearly 700 square miles) of ice—representing a **loss of over 10% to 14% of its total surface area** in a historically brief window.
* **Structural Failure:** The recent cracking has severed a narrow, 40-kilometer-long ice bridge that previously connected the main shelf to Charcot and Latady islands. The destruction of this natural buttress has exposed the remaining inner shelf to ocean waves, accelerating the potential for total collapse.

### Contrast with Historical Stability Since the 1930s

The sudden disintegration of the Wilkins Ice Shelf stands in sharp contrast to its long-documented history. First discovered and mapped during aerial expeditions in the 1930s, the ice shelf maintained a constant, stable boundary for most of the 20th century. Glaciological records show that while smaller seasonal calving occurred, the shelf's core structure remained intact and anchored for at least 80 years.

"The Wilkins Ice Shelf had been stable for all of recorded history since the 1930s," noted ESA glaciology researchers. "What we are observing now is an extraordinary rate of fragmentation that has never been documented in this region before."

### Driver of the Collapse

Scientists attribute the rapid crack propagation to unprecedented atmospheric and oceanic warming along the Antarctic Peninsula. Over the past 50 years, the region has experienced a temperature rise of nearly 3 degrees Celsius (5.4 degrees Fahrenheit)—one of the fastest rates of warming on the planet.

As surface meltwater pools on top of the shelf, it fills existing micro-fractures. The weight of this water acts like a wedge—a process known as hydrofracturing—forcing the cracks to drive deeper into the ice until massive bergs break away.

While the loss of the Wilkins Ice Shelf itself will not significantly raise global sea levels (as the ice shelf is already floating on ocean water), scientists warn that its destabilization removes a crucial barrier. Without the shelf to hold them back, inland glaciers could accelerate their flow into the sea, directly contributing to global sea-level rise. ESA satellites will continue around-the-clock radar monitoring of the remaining ice structure.
